Removing build.rs will remove go build from cargo lifecycle. The file is still incomplete though, I have to add few functionalities and assert checks for it. Build.rs is a common practice in Rust to build external language dependencies like cc, cxx, swift, etc.
Regarding cargo zig build should be able to build rn, because the dependencies are under compat. But worth to keep an eye on it

Also is counter productive run go build and cargo build for every change on opencode. Are you asking it because of concerns for goreleaser? We can also add a cargo env parameter that allow receive the binary from a specific source. Many build.rs does that

In this case we might just use if cases instead of a switch and order the priority as we want

> I see in the video above that you can scroll down and there is empty space why is that ? @kujtimiihoxha The diffview accepts an `yOffset` option to skip (scroll) a given number of lines from the top. We're simply mimicing modern code editors that allow you to scroll beyond the end of the file. Remember that diffview will be a generic standard component, and that may be nice in some scenarios. Andrey this is absolutely incredible. I'd make two changes:

1. I'd add bind <kbd>shift+hjkl</kbd> to the navigation bindings
2. Currently you can scroll horizontally and vertically endlessly. I'd change it so that scrolling stops when there's no more content to show, so you essentially can't scroll endlessly.

I'm on the fence about scrolling beyond the bounds, but let's keep it for now and get a feel for it.

no strong opinions either way, but, we should probably have a "standard" for that internally.

## Image Pasting in Claude Code vs Cursor

### Claude Code
Claude Code supports image pasting through multiple methods:
1. **Drag and drop** - Drop an image file into the Claude Code window
2. **Clipboard paste** - Copy an image and paste it using **Ctrl+V** (not Cmd+V on Mac)
3. **File path reference** - Provide a path like `/path/to/image.png`

The documentation specifically mentions using **Ctrl+V** for pasting images from clipboard.

### Cursor IDE
Cursor also supports image pasting but with some limitations:
- **Chat area**: Full Ctrl+V clipboard support for images
- **Edit box**: Limited support - requires drag & drop or saving image first, then referencing it with @ symbol
- Users can take screenshots and paste directly into chat for visual communication

### The Issue
It seems like there might be a keybinding conflict where Ctrl+V is opening nvim instead of pasting the image. This could be:
1. A terminal/shell configuration issue (iTerm2/zsh keybindings)
2. A conflict with system keybindings
3. A potential issue with how crush handles the Ctrl+V shortcut

### Suggested Investigation
- Check if this happens in other terminals besides iTerm2
- Test with different shell configurations
- Verify if crush is properly handling the Ctrl+V keybinding for image paste vs text paste

* Add a new provider `type`, say `openai-responses`, that converts the whole provider to using the new API.
* Add a model flag, so this can be switched on just for certain models, such as the new models that require it.

As @hutchisr pointed out, this is going to mean entering a game of cat-and-mouse with Anthropic. It's not a matter of just implementing OAuth support; you have to keep up with Anthropic's defensive practices, which now include checking each API request used with a subscription token to try detect whether the request is coming from Claude Code - not just through "spoofable" things like headers, but by the _content that gets sent to the model_.

There are workarounds at the moment (which OpenCode is rightly hesitant to detail - https://github.com/sst/opencode/issues/417#issuecomment-3010089994) but in the long run Anthropic will almost certainly win this battle if they want to. To the fullest extent of their existing practices, you can literally only use these subscription tokens if your request includes the full Claude Code system prompt and toolset, which is proprietary, and even aside from it being proprietary, it influences model behavior which will harm anyone's (Crush, OpenCode, etc.) ability to differentiate _their_ coding agent from Claude Code.

To be clear, I want this too, just don't blame Crush for not doing this yet, as if it's easy or just an oversight. :) The pressure should really be on Anthropic imo.

According to the [GitHub Copilot Extension Developer Policy](https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/github-terms/github-copilot-extension-developer-policy#2-developing-your-extension), section 2:

> ... Extensions and developers must not:
> - Degrade or compromise security
> - Bypass or circumvent protocols and access controls
> - **Use unpublished APIs**

(emphasis mine)

GitHub doesn't publish an official Copilot API, and instead exposes its functionality through first party extensions and services. All unofficial wrappers access this unpublished API, which is in direct violation of this policy.

Edit: and as I mentioned above, it is possible to use copilot with crush through the use of [`copilot-api`](https://github.com/ericc-ch/copilot-api) which wraps these unpublished APIs into an OpenAI compatible server. @anuramat was kind enough to provide the crush config required to do that.

For anyone else investigating this: The problem is that the entire candidate list is generated pre-hoc (including all recursive files!), doing this in e.g. a large monorepo just blows up everything (and caching will also not help in this case, as the original operation will already block for a long time or never even complete).

A "proper" fix is actually quite difficult, for example: The completion logic could be refactored to be able to lazily generate the candidate list (e.g. read from the filesystem with a non-strict iterator, cache all seen files during the completion, and lazily load more so that there's always ~10 candidates available). Doing this correctly is not easy.

A much simpler way would be to not do fuzzy matching on the full path, and complete individual path segments instead. But this is a functionality change ...

If crush doesn't show Qwen3 Coder (free) even after editing crush.json, the issue is likely that Crush overwrites its own providers.json at runtime.

Root Cause: Crush replaces your config with its internal default unless you patch the installed package's providers.json.

Fix Summary:

1, Locate Crush install dir:


C:\Users\(put your username here)\AppData\Roaming\npm\node_modules\@charmland\crush
In that folder, edit or replace providers.json to include:


{
  "id": "qwen/qwen3-coder:free",
  "name": "Qwen: Qwen3 Coder (free)",
  "cost_per_1m_in": 0,
  "cost_per_1m_out": 0,
  "context_window": 262144,
  "default_max_tokens": 32768,
  ...
}

2, And update the provider's default_small_model_id to:


"default_small_model_id": "qwen/qwen3-coder:free"

3, Prevent future overwrites with PowerShell:

attrib +R "C:\Users\(put your username here)\AppData\Roaming\npm\node_modules\@charmland\crush\providers.json"
attrib +R "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\crush\providers.json"
Restart Crush — the model should now persist across sessions.

Pro tip: Backup the folder first in case you need to restore defaults.

This is working for me, thank you!   Noting current STDIO behavior in case other people start looking:

 * If one starts a STDIO MCP server, the process will stay alive after the tool call and show the Green Dot.
 * If that MCP server process is killed, the Crush MCP Green Dot will remain.  Crush doesn't know the transport state unless it tries to read/write periodically ([MCP ping](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-03-26/basic/utilities/ping)).
 * If the STDIO MCP Server is dead, a new process is created and everything works fine (assuming it starts properly). I don't think there is logging of its demise.

Note, this required 4 internal tools to be added, not 2, to work correctly. Crush has a bad habit of trying to incorrectly guess the names of the lsp and mcp servers that are running, and had no introspection into their names before. So, in addition to the restart tools (1 mcp, 1 lsp) I added a tool for listing the mcps and one for listing the lsps.

Right now, permissions for these tools are manually granted. If we want, we can enable the list permission to be granted automatically, since it's non-destructive. 

Same goes for restarting the LSPs/MCPs, but it's probably best to request permissions for that, since it kills running processes and restarts them.

@jamestrew, Thanks for the feedback! For some context: in the **Discord discussions** with the maintainers and contributors (Christian, Kujtim, Manu, JD, and others), it was agreed that `@` should remain **reserved for a future feature**, so it’s not suitable to use it right now for file references.

That’s why the consolidated proposal is:

* `/` → quick commands (e.g., `/exit`, `/mcp`)
* `#` → references to files already indexed in the project (with line support, e.g., `#src/main.py:42`)
* `~` → paths relative to the project root (e.g., `~docs/guide.md`)
* `>` → direct shell/script execution (e.g., `>npm run dev`)
* `f:` → quick file search by name (e.g., `f:config.json`)

### Key points discussed on Discord:

* **Christian** and **Kujtim**: gave positive feedback and supported the proposal, even pinning the message as reference.
* **JD**: emphasized that using `@` for files creates conflicts in tools like Claude Code, slowing things down in large projects.
* **Manu**: suggested using `!` for shell commands (as in Vim/Neovim and Jupyter). We debated pros and cons, and agreed that `>` avoids conflicts (with Bash history, logical operators, Git, etc.) and ensures predictability across all environments.
* **Kujtim**: asked about the difference between `#` and `~`. We aligned that `#` always refers to a file already indexed in the project context (with full integration), while `~` is just a literal path relative to the root, including docs and assets outside the workspace.

This mapping was designed to **reduce the learning curve**, **avoid collisions**, and create a clear and consistent grammar in Crush—benefiting both CLI and IDE users.

I've opened https://github.com/charmbracelet/crush/pull/914, which takes a step in this direction.

It doesn't let you add your own subagents. It turns out though that Crush already has one hardcoded subagent - the task subagent. The top-level "coder" agent can defer open ended "find how this works" or "find where this is implemented" style tasks to the "task" agent.

My main goal with #914 was to let you pick which model which agent uses. As part of that though I've updated the sidebar and splash screen to show what agents exist and what models they're using.

I've also added an `agents` config block that currently just lets you configure the model for the two built in agents. I could imagine a future PR extending the agents block to allow you to:

* Define new agents
* Specify what model they should use
* Specify what tools they can use

# Comment for GitHub Issues #472 and #727

## Investigation Findings: Root Causes of Compaction Hanging

I've done a deep dive into the codebase and found several critical issues causing the compaction hanging behavior:

### 🐛 Critical Bug Found

There's a bug in `/internal/llm/agent/agent.go` line 814 where error handling uses an undefined variable:

```go
// Current (BROKEN):
Error: fmt.Errorf("failed to summarize: %w", err)  // 'err' is undefined!

// Should be:
Error: fmt.Errorf("failed to summarize: %w", r.Error)
```

**This bug prevents ANY error messages from being shown during compaction failures**, which explains why you're seeing "nothing happens" - errors are occurring but not being displayed!

### ⏱️ No Timeouts

The compaction process has no timeout configured. It uses `context.WithCancel()` instead of `context.WithTimeout()`, meaning it can run forever if the provider doesn't respond or is very slow.

### 📊 No Progress Feedback

The UI only shows generic messages like "Compacting Session..." without any details about:
- Token count being processed
- Time elapsed
- Retry attempts
- Provider status

### For OpenRouter users (#472)

OpenRouter errors (rate limits, provider issues) are being swallowed by the bug above. The providers might be failing but you'll never see the error.

### For Ollama users (#727)

Local models like Qwen3 0.6b can be VERY slow for summarization tasks, especially with limited context (2048 tokens). Without timeout or progress feedback, it appears frozen even if it's actually processing.

## Workarounds (until fixed)

1. **Check logs**: Run crush with `--debug` flag and check `~/.local/share/crush/logs/crush.log` for actual errors
2. **Smaller sessions**: Try to compact before reaching high context usage
3. **Faster models**: If using Ollama, try a faster/larger model for summarization if possible

## Proposed Fix

I've documented the complete fix in a separate issue, but the immediate changes needed are:
1. Fix the error variable bug (one-line change)
2. Add a 5-minute timeout
3. Show progress updates every few seconds

- We did not use the main loop context so when you cancel the request or the main agent is done the loop was continuing.

Not sure when they'll work on that, I'm sure they're busy with everything, but here's my current workaround:

## Basic Bypass Script

Create the bypass script:
```bash
touch /usr/local/bin/bypass
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/bypass
```

Edit `/usr/local/bin/bypass` with this content:
```bash
#!/bin/bash
if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Usage: bypass <command> [args...]"
    exit 1
fi

"$@"
```

This tricks Crush into thinking we're running a custom command called "bypass" when we're really just piping things through.

## Handling `sudo`

```bash
#!/bin/bash
if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Usage: bypass <command> [args...]"
    exit 1
fi

COMMAND="$1"
shift
if [ "$COMMAND" = "sudo" ]; then
    if sudo -n true 2>/dev/null; then
        exec sudo "$@"
    else
        if command -v zenity >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            PASSWORD=$(zenity --password --title="Authentication Required" --text="Enter password for sudo:" 2>/dev/null)
            if [ $? -eq 0 ] && [ -n "$PASSWORD" ]; then
                echo "$PASSWORD" | sudo -S "$@" 2>/dev/null
            else
                exit 1
            fi
        else
            echo "Error: zenity not found for GUI password prompt"
            exit 1
        fi
    fi
else
    "$COMMAND" "$@"
fi
```

This simply makes `bypass sudo` calls use `zenity`, which is a GUI `sudo` handler that won't corrupt Crush's terminal interface.

Make sure you install `zenity` though (e.g., `sudo apt install zenity`).

## Configure Crush

Add this to your `~/.config/crush/CRUSH.md` so Crush knows the `bypass` command exists:

```markdown
## Security Commands
When running restricted commands for security purposes, use the `bypass` script:
- `bypass sudo <command>` - for `sudo` operations
- `bypass <any-restricted-command>` - for other security-restricted commands
```

Make sure you have `"context_paths": ["$HOME/.config/crush/CRUSH.md"]` in your `~/.config/crush/crush.json`.

@kujtimiihoxha I did just append `memory_paths` to `context_paths` at first, but then realised the coder prompt explicitly tells the LLM that everything in there is project context files, which isn't accurate for the memory files. My thinking with separating them was more clearly conveying to the model that the user's preferences might need to override the project's and ensuring the overrides appear after what they're overriding seemed ideal.

Distinguishing between upstream project context and user-local project context might be useful as well (but at least as a separate PR); for example, Crush's `CRUSH.md` includes instructions to use `task`, but that executable is named `go-task` on my system. I have a `CRUSH.local.md` telling it to use `go-task` over `task`, but the model often still calls `task` instead of `go-task`. Maybe including upstream project context, then local project context with a note that these might need to override the upstream context, then user preferences with a note that these might need to override everything else would more cleanly solve that than more user-side prompts.

Thanks for the thorough review, @meowgorithm — all five findings are addressed in 26399fc.

**P1 — browser flow inherited the 15s connection timeout.** `createSession` now hands the OAuth handler a hook to stop the connection-timeout timer, and `Authorize` calls it the moment authorization starts, then runs the flow under its own 3-minute deadline. Login/consent can no longer be cancelled by the connection timeout.

**P1 — persisted tokens couldn't refresh.** The handler now performs dynamic client registration itself (`oauthex.RegisterClient`) and passes the result to the SDK as a *pre-registered* client, so the real client ID/secret, endpoints, and auth style are captured and persisted alongside the token (no more empty client ID). On restart the restored `oauth2.Config` has everything it needs to refresh. New test `TestMCPOAuthHandler_RestoredTokenRefreshes` drives an expired token through a real refresh and asserts the persisted client ID is sent.

**P1 — concurrent init could lose credentials.** All handlers in a process now share one `tokenStore` (single mutex) keyed by config path via `sharedTokenStore`, and `save()` re-reads and merges the on-disk file before writing so a concurrent writer's entries survive. Covered by `TestTokenStore_ConcurrentSavePreservesEntries` (run under `-race`) and `TestSharedTokenStore_SameInstancePerPath`.

**P2 — non-OAuth 403 replaced a valid token with `nil`.** `Authorize` now short-circuits a non-`insufficient_scope` 403 exactly like the SDK does (returns `nil` to retry) before touching any state, and never overwrites `tokenSrc` with a nil source. Dug into this properly (thanks for the patience). Root cause traced to a real gap in `charm.land/fantasy`, the shared provider/retry library crush depends on — not something fixable inside crush's own codebase alone.

**What's actually happening:** the `nemotron 3 ultra free` / OpenCode Zen error you saw is a mid-stream, in-band SSE error event (the stream already returned 200 OK before it fails). openai-go's SDK only wraps errors on the *initial* HTTP response as `*openai.Error` — its own doc comment says "other errors are not wrapped by this SDK." A mid-stream error instead comes back as a different type (`*ssestream.StreamError`), which fantasy's error-conversion code didn't recognize at all. So this class of error was never being classified as retryable — it wasn't just marked "don't retry," it was invisible to the retry system entirely, which is why it stalled with no recovery attempt.

**Fix:** opened charmbracelet/fantasy#319 — parses the stream error's JSON body and converts it to a real `*ProviderError`, treating `type:"server_error"` as retryable so fantasy's existing exponential-backoff retry engages for this case. Full test suite passes (1374 tests), added 3 new regression tests covering the exact error shape from this report.

Once that merges (or a fantasy version bump picks it up), crush gets provider-aware retry for this specific failure mode for free, no crush-side change needed for the retry piece itself.

Still want to look separately at item 2 from my original comment — better UX for a partial-stream failure (explicit "partial output, retrying" state) — as a crush-side follow-up once the retry fix lands upstream, so a user isn't just watching a silent multi-second pause during the backoff.

## Review findings — all addressed

Each finding is fixed in an individual commit with regression tests. Tests for bugs/security issues are written to fail before the fix (red→green). Full suite passes under `-race` for all touched packages.

### Finding 1 [P0] — channel events as false state changes
**Commit:** `2cb0bdb2`

`mcpEventTypeToProto`'s default branch mapped every unknown type (including `EventChannelMessage`) to `MCPEventStateChanged`, so each channel notification became a spurious state change for SSE clients. Now returns `""` for unsupported types; `wrapEvent` drops them instead of fabricating an envelope. Channel messages still publish to the in-process broker (for tests + PR 2) but no longer leak through the client/server wire.

**Tests:** `TestMCPChannelMessageNotWrappedAsStateChange`, `TestMCPUnknownEventTypeNotMappedToStateChange`

### Finding 2 [P1] — process-global channel state
**Commit:** `1f623ec0`

The MCP broker is process-global and every `app.App` subscribes via `SubscribeEvents`. Channel events carry no workspace/session identity, so forwarding them through the shared fan-out would let one workspace's channel messages reach every other workspace. `SubscribeEvents` now filters `EventChannelMessage` so channel events do not reach the per-app event broker. The in-process broker still carries them for tests and PR 2 delivery; workspace-scoped routing is deferred to PR 2.

**Tests:** `TestSubscribeEventsFiltersChannelMessages`

### Finding 3 [P1] — channel first-wins mismatch
**Commit:** `a09cb366`

`logFirstWinsMismatch` omitted `EnabledChannels` from the comparison, so a second client that inherited (or lost) a channel silently did so. Now compared and logged alongside YOLO, Debug, DataDir, and Env.

**Tests:** `TestFirstWinsMismatch_LogsOnFlagDifferences/channels`

### Finding 4 [P1] — dispatch completion-boundary race
**Commit:** `fbf59341`

`Run`'s deferred `activeRequests.Del` fired unconditionally on function return. When a finishing run handed off to a queued prompt (or a concurrent caller registered in the window between the explicit Del and the deferred Del), the stale cleanup wiped the new run's cancel — breaking `Cancel()` and potentially allowing concurrent turns.

Wrapped the cancel in an `activeCancel` struct with pointer identity and replaced the unconditional `Del` with `CompareAndDelete` (added to `csync.Map`). The deferred cleanup now only fires when the stored entry is still ours.

**Tests:** `TestMap_CompareAndDelete` (csync), `TestRun_CompletionBoundaryDoesNotWipeNextRunCancel` (agent)

### Finding 5 [P1] — notifications lost during initialization
**Commit:** `bc8ff341`

The SDK read loop starts inside `client.Connect`, but the gate opened only after Connect returned. A fast server's events were silently swallowed while the gate was closed. Replaced the boolean gate with a three-state `channelGate` (undecided → open/closed). Notifications arriving while undecided are buffered; resolving to open drains the buffer, resolving to closed discards it (fail closed).

**Tests:** `TestChannelConnBuffersDuringUndecidedGate`, `TestChannelConnDiscardsBufferOnClosedGate`

### Finding 6 [P2] — malformed/structurally altered XML from meta keys
**Commit:** `fed86b00`

The key pattern accepted names beginning with digits (`1chat`), which are not valid XML names — `encoding/xml` emitted them without error, producing structurally altered output. Also permitted namespace-sensitive names (`xmlns`, `xml`). Now requires a letter/underscore start (`^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$`) and rejects the reserved namespace family.

**Tests:** `TestParseChannelParams/meta_key_starting_with_digit_dropped`, `TestParseChannelParams/xmlns_meta_key_dropped`, `TestParseChannelParams/xml_meta_key_dropped`

### Finding 7 [P2] — lossy broker for channel delivery
**Commit:** `f7c53cbc`

`publishChannelMessage` used lossy `Broker.Publish` — a burst or stalled subscriber could permanently lose chat messages or alerts. Switched to `PublishMustDeliver` (bounded-blocking, timeout-bounded, drops counted at ERROR). Threaded the `Read` context through so delivery respects session cancellation.

**Tests:** `TestPublishChannelMessageUsesMustDeliver`

### Finding 8 [P2] — `--channels` unavailable to `crush run`
**Commit:** `ca9ef6ad`

The flag was registered with `rootCmd.Flags()` (local), not `PersistentFlags()`. Subcommands don't inherit local flags, so `crush run --channels server:webhook` failed with "unknown flag." Moved to `PersistentFlags()` so both `crush` and `crush run` accept it.

**Tests:** `TestChannelsFlagAvailableOnRunCmd`, `TestChannelsFlagAvailableOnRootCmd`

---

**Verification:** `go build ./...`, `go vet` on changed packages, and `go test -race` on all changed packages (agent, mcp, backend, server, cmd, csync) pass clean. Two pre-existing failures in `internal/config` (`TestRefreshOAuthToken_*`) are unrelated to this PR — they fail on the base commit too.

Dug into this since it's a great writeup — traced the exec path and tried to reproduce the exact mechanism (mvdan/sh's POSIX tokenizer eating backslashes from a substituted $HOME) before proposing a fix.

Couldn't reproduce it, and I don't think the described mechanism is actually what's happening. Standard POSIX shell behavior (and mvdan/sh follows it): backslash-escape processing happens during the initial parse of the literal source text, before any expansions run. Tilde/parameter expansion results are substituted in afterward and are not re-scanned for escape sequences — this is intentional in POSIX shells generally (it's part of why variable contents don't get re-interpreted as shell syntax). So a `~` that expands to a backslash-containing HOME shouldn't hit the tokenizer's escape logic at all.

Tested two ways with `HOME` set to a real Windows path with backslashes (e.g. `C:\Users\alice`):
1. Through crush's shell with a builtin (`cat ~/marker.txt`) — resolved correctly.
2. Through a real external `bash.exe` subprocess (git-bash's actual MSYS binary) invoked the same way your repro does (`bash ~/marker.sh`) — also resolved correctly.

Also checked: `internal/shell/` and `internal/hooks/` have zero commits between the `v0.85.0` you tested against and current `main` — so this isn't a case where it was already fixed upstream since you filed it. The code you tested is what I just tested.

Given that, this looks like it might be environment-specific rather than a bug in crush's shell layer as described — a couple of concrete possibilities:
- A different MSYS/git-bash runtime version with different argv/env path-translation behavior than what I have (Git for Windows has shipped different MSYS runtime versions over time)
- crush launched directly from an active git-bash terminal session (inheriting live MSYS environment state) vs. a plain cmd/PowerShell parent — I couldn't fully replicate the former in a test harness

Would help to narrow this down:
1. Output of `bash --version` on your machine
2. Whether you launched crush from inside a git-bash/MSYS terminal, or from cmd.exe/PowerShell
3. The literal (redacted is fine, e.g. `C:\Users\XXXXX`) value logged for the corrupted path, so I can check for anything beyond simple backslash-loss

Happy to keep digging with that info — didn't want to merge a fix for a mechanism I couldn't actually verify.

@meowgorithm Good question, and the answer turns out to be "better than you'd fear in one place, worse in another." Rebased onto `main` while I was in here, so the conflicts are cleared too.

**Short version: there's no Bash string-parsing involved in blocking.** The block list is installed as `mvdan/sh` `interp.ExecHandler` middleware (`blockHandler` in `internal/shell/run.go`), so it runs once per command the interpreter *actually executes*, and it sees the fully-expanded `argv`. Your two examples are both caught. I ran them to be sure:

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `SOME_VAR=true && cd ~/some/path && scp ./file` | BLOCKED |
| `cd ~/some/path && curl -i https://example.com > response.txt` | BLOCKED |

The expansion happening before we see it means some less obvious ones are covered for free:

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `CMD=curl; $CMD --version` | BLOCKED |
| `eval "curl --version"` | BLOCKED |
| `command curl --version` / `\curl --version` | BLOCKED |
| `if true; then curl --version; fi` | BLOCKED |
| `echo hi \| curl --version` | BLOCKED |

**One real hole your question did shake loose**, now fixed in `092d4da2`: `CommandsBlocker` compared `argv[0]` verbatim, so `/usr/bin/curl` and `./curl` walked right past a rule written for `curl`. It now normalizes to the basename first — and on Windows also handles backslash separators and strips the `.exe`/`.bat` extension, since `C:\…\curl.exe` has the same problem.

**What it still can't do**, which I've documented in the README rather than pretended away: anything that reaches a binary through another program is out of reach by construction — `sh -c "curl …"`, `python -c`, `make`, `find -exec`, and wrappers like `env curl` / `nohup curl` where `argv[0]` is the wrapper. An `argv[0]` deny list can't close that, so the README now frames it as a guardrail against a model casually reaching for the wrong tool, not a security boundary around an untrusted one. Happy to reword if you'd rather it read differently.

---

Separately — chasing this down led me to something worse in the *other* matching layer, which I've written up in #3425 rather than pile into this PR. Short version: the permission auto-approve path (`isSafeReadOnly` in `internal/agent/tools/bash.go`) *is* naive `strings.HasPrefix` matching, guarded by a chaining check that misses newline, bare `&`, redirections and process substitution. So these all skip the permission prompt entirely on current `main`:

```bash
echo pwned > ~/.bashrc
echo hi & rm -rf /tmp/pwned
env rm -rf /tmp/pwned
git remote set-url origin https://evil.example/x.git
```

That last one seemed worth flagging loudly. The fix is the AST pre-pass you're implicitly suggesting — `syntax.Parser`, fail closed on anything not provably inert. I'm working on it now and will send it as its own PR against #3425 so this one stays a small config change.

Full behavior delta for this PR, in both directions, with the reasoning on each. I generated this by running the old prefix matcher and the new one side by side over the same inputs rather than reasoning about it, so it should be exhaustive for the cases below.

Also pushed two follow-ups since opening: `eb44bb2e` fixes the staticcheck `QF1001` that was failing lint, and `e2671fb6` restores three read-only git forms that the rebuilt list had cost (detailed under "fixed" below).

## Commands that used to prompt and now don't

Two, both the same root cause:

| Command | Why |
|---|---|
| `ls; pwd` | A sequence of individually read-only statements is itself read-only. The old matcher rejected `;` outright while *accepting* a newline, which is the same node to the parser — so this was inconsistent rather than deliberate. |
| `ls\npwd` | Same. Note the old matcher accepted `echo hi\nrm -rf /` (because `echo` is followed by a space) but rejected `ls\npwd` (because `ls` is followed by the newline itself). That inconsistency was the prefix rule, not a policy. |

Nothing else got more permissive. `time ls` and `nohup ls -la` read as newly-allowed if you only look at the safe list, but both auto-approved before too — they're unchanged.

## Commands that used to work and now prompt

**Intended — these are the bug.** Each skipped the prompt entirely before:

| Command | Why it now prompts |
|---|---|
| `echo pwned > ~/.bashrc` | Redirection is an arbitrary file write. `echo` is only safe because redirects are now rejected. |
| `echo hi & rm -rf /tmp/x` | The old chaining scan listed `&&` but not bare `&`. |
| `ls <(rm -rf /tmp/x)` | Process substitution runs a command; it wasn't in the metacharacter list. |
| `env rm -rf /tmp/x` | `env` was on the safe list and runs whatever it's handed. Now peeled — `env ls` still auto-approves. |
| `nohup curl https://evil.example` | Same wrapper problem, and it also defeated the block list. `nohup ls -la` still auto-approves. |
| `timeout 5 rm -rf /tmp/x` | Same. `timeout 5 ls` still auto-approves. |
| `git branch -D main` | The prefix rule accepted `-` as a delimiter, so every flag came along with `git branch`. |
| `git tag -d v1` | Same. |
| `git remote set-url origin <url>` | Same; silently repoints the remote so the next `git push` goes elsewhere. |
| `git config --get-urlmatch a b` | `--get-urlmatch` matched the `git config --get` prefix. Flags are now matched exactly. |
| `git diff --ext-diff` | Runs the repo's configured external diff driver. |

**Deliberate policy calls** — these were genuinely usable before and now cost a prompt:

| Command | Why |
|---|---|
| `kill -9 123`, `killall node` | Signal arbitrary processes, including ones the user is relying on. Read-only was never the right description. |
| `set -x`, `unset PATH` | Mutate shell state. `unset PATH` in particular changes how later commands resolve. |
| `git ls-remote <url>` | Makes a network call. Sits badly next to a block list that bans `curl`/`wget`; happy to put it back if you'd rather weigh convenience higher. |
| `hostname myhost` | Bare `hostname` reads and still auto-approves; with an operand it *sets* the hostname. |
| `date -s 2020-01-01` | Sets the system clock. Bare `date` and `date +%Y-%m-%d` still auto-approve. |

**Conservatism cost** — the one category I'd call a genuine regression rather than a fix:

| Command | Why |
|---|---|
| `echo $HOME`, `ls $HOME`, `echo hi $USER` | Parameter expansion isn't resolved during the check, so the final argv isn't knowable and the command can't be shown to be inert. Modelling expansion here would mean reimplementing a chunk of the shell, and getting it subtly wrong is exactly the failure this PR exists to remove — so it fails closed instead. This is the change most likely to be felt day to day, and it's the one I'd most welcome pushback on. |

## Regressions I fixed rather than shipped (`e2671fb6`)

Rebuilding the list initially cost three read-only forms their auto-approval. All three are back:

- `git branch --contains <commit>`, `git branch --merged <ref>`
- `git tag --points-at <ref>`, `git tag --contains <commit>`
- `git remote show <name>`, `git remote get-url <name>`

The branch/tag entries reject operands, because that's what keeps `git branch <name>` and `git tag <name>` — which *create* — prompting. The fix reuses the `requireFlag` mechanism already used for `git config --get`: a filter flag must be present, and the filter flag is exactly what distinguishes listing from creating. git itself refuses to mix a filter flag with branch creation, so the two can't be combined into a mutation. The read-only `remote` subcommands are spelled out individually so `add`/`remove`/`rename`/`set-url`/`prune` stay off.

## Unchanged, for completeness

`git config user.name attacker` reads like a fix but was already prompting — `git config --get` never prefix-matched it. Likewise `git -c core.pager=sh log` was rejected before and after.

Thanks everyone for digging into this! 🙏 I've confirmed the behavior on both terminals and wanted to close the loop.

## Confirmed behavior

**Ghostty (macOS):** `Cmd+Shift+click` opens the URL. Ghostty's `mouse-shift-capture` option defaults to `false`, so holding **Shift bypasses mouse capture** by full-screen TUI apps, and **Cmd** then triggers Ghostty's URL handler. Config docs: https://ghostty.org/docs/config/reference (`mouse-shift-capture`, `mouse-reporting`). Ghostty also fully supports OSC 8 hyperlinks: https://ghostty.org/docs/vt/osc/8

**Kitty (macOS):** `Shift+click` opens the URL. Kitty's default `mouse_map` includes:
```
mouse_map shift+left click grabbed,ungrabbed mouse_handle_click selection link prompt
```
so plain **Shift+Click** handles links even when an app has grabbed the mouse (no Cmd needed). Config docs: https://sw.kovidgoyal.net/kitty/conf/ (`detect_urls`, `mouse_map`). Kitty supports OSC 8 hyperlinks via `underline_hyperlinks` / `show_hyperlink_targets` in the same config.

## Conclusion

This is expected terminal behavior for full-screen TUI apps that capture the mouse, not a Crush bug! Crush is already emitting well-formed OSC 8 sequences (as @albatrossflyon-coder verified end-to-end through glamour → ultraviolet → the final buffer). The issue is purely the modifier required to bypass mouse capture differs per terminal.

Same class of problem here, and it's broader than tool-call budgets. Running an opencode-based orchestration setup (this repo's architecture family) with heavy subagent usage, I regularly see subagents hang for hours with zero visible progress:

1. **Invalid model / provider config** - the subagent silently retries forever. My logs show hundreds of ProviderModelNotFoundError + connect-timeout errors piling up over days; the parent session just sits there waiting with no status surface.
2. **Permission prompts nobody can answer** - exactly what #3365 describes; I hit a multi-hour stall from this too.
3. **No stop propagation** - cancelling the parent task doesn't reliably kill descendant subagents; they keep burning tokens/connections in the background.

Concrete proposals that would address the whole class:

1. **Hard-enforced per-task timeout** - configurable in config (crush.json) with a per-task override. On expiry: kill the subagent session, surface partial output + exit reason to the parent, let the parent decide retry/fallback instead of waiting forever.
2. **Progress heartbeat** - expose per-subagent activity to the parent view (last tool call, step count, tokens spent) so the user can tell working from stuck without waiting hours to find out.
3. **Tool-call/step budget as a hard cap, not a prompt directive** - e.g. maxSteps: 50; terminate and report when exceeded. This issue shows models ignore soft instructions.
4. **Cancel cascade + resource cleanup** - user cancel (or parent abort) must propagate through the whole agent tree and reclaim session slots/connections so aborted runs don't linger.

These are orthogonal to #3365 (permissions) and complement the noninteractive fix. Happy to help spec or test.

Still reproduces on **v0.88.0**, and I think the scope is wider than tool-call chunks — plus there's an observability problem that makes it much harder to diagnose than it needs to be.

## No tool call is required

The original repro pauses *between tool-call chunks*. But a provider that opens the SSE stream and simply never sends a terminating chunk hangs the same way — no tool call involved at all.

Minimal mock (Python stdlib only):

```python
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer
import time
class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, *a): pass
    def do_POST(self):
        self.rfile.read(int(self.headers.get('Content-Length') or 0))
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
        self.end_headers()
        time.sleep(3600)          # headers sent, body never arrives
ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8899), H).serve_forever()
```

```bash
timeout 30 crush run --cwd ./ws -m myprov/mymodel "say OK"; echo "EXIT=$?"
# EXIT=124
```

A variant that streams only `reasoning_content` deltas and never emits `content` behaves identically.

## The part that cost us the most: zero bytes on both streams

`crush run` produces **0 bytes on stdout and 0 bytes on stderr** for the entire hang — including with `--debug`. From an operator's seat this is indistinguishable from a crashed binary, a bad API key, or a DNS failure. We spent a while chasing credentials before realising the process was alive and simply waiting.

Three things combine to make it fully silent:

1. `internal/cmd/root.go` sets `slog.SetDefault(slog.New(slog.DiscardHandler))` on entry, so everything before the file logger is initialised is dropped. (There's already a `FIXME` on it.)
2. `--debug` raises the level but still routes to `<DataDirectory>/logs/crush.log`, never to the console. Only `run --verbose` mirrors to stderr, and that happens *after* workspace setup.
3. `internal/app/app.go` prints `msg.Content().String()`, which returns `TextContent` only — so `ReasoningContent` never reaches stdout. A model that is still "thinking" looks like a model that is doing nothing.

The spinner is TTY-gated, so in a script or under `timeout` there is no signal at all.

## Diagnostic signature (may help others land here)

`HTTP Request` appears in `crush.log` with no matching `HTTP Response`:

```bash
crush --debug run -m prov/model "say OK"
python3 - <<'EOF'
import json
req = resp = 0
for line in open('.crush/logs/crush.log'):
    try: d = json.loads(line)
    except ValueError: continue
    if d.get('msg') == 'HTTP Request':  req += 1
    if d.get('msg') == 'HTTP Response': resp += 1
print('req=', req, 'resp=', resp)
EOF
```

`req > 0 && resp == 0` means the stream never completed. This works because `drainBody()` in `internal/log/http.go` reads the response body to completion **before** logging it — so a stalled stream produces no `HTTP Response` line at all, ever.

## Suggestions

Beyond the bounded stream/read timeout already requested here:

- Emit a stderr warning after N seconds of stream inactivity, even without `--verbose`. Silence is the real trap; a single line like `no stream activity for 60s` would have ended our investigation immediately.
- Consider having `run` exit non-zero with a diagnostic on stream timeout rather than relying on the caller's `timeout`.

## Environment

- `crush version v0.88.0` (npm `@charmland/crush@0.88.0`)
- Linux x86_64, Ubuntu 24.04
- Local mock provider; no external service required.

Hit this in production today. Adding a concrete deployment case and some measurements, since the thread so far is mostly "just wrap it".

## Deployment

Crush runs as the agent provider behind a Telegram bridge that operates a small fleet of Linux nodes. The operator talks to it in a private chat; it is the sole allowlisted user, and the host policy is already "full access" — the equivalent Codex lane runs with `approval=never` + `dangerFullAccess`, and the bridge auto-approves every permission request.

So the operator has explicitly opted into full trust, at every layer that offers a knob.

## What is actually unreachable

The bans are not an edge case for this workload — they remove most of what the agent exists to do:

| Task | Blocked by |
|---|---|
| Reach another node | `ssh`, `scp` |
| Restart its own service after an update | `systemctl`, `service` |
| Install a dependency | `apt`, `apt-get`, `dnf`, `pacman`, … |
| Check an endpoint | `curl`, `wget` |
| Inspect networking | `ip`, `ifconfig`, `netstat` |

The `systemctl` one is worth calling out. A self-managing agent that pulls an update cannot restart itself, and the guidance it produces is to hand the command back to the human — which is exactly the loop the deployment exists to remove.

## Measured behaviour (v0.88.0)

It is two mechanisms, not one:

1. `bashDescription` interpolates `{{ .BannedCommands }}` into the tool description, so the model is *told* the list and refuses on its own. Our run produced a polite explanation and no tool call at all:

   > The `ssh` command is blocked by my security policy (it's in the banned commands list), so I can't execute it directly.

2. `blockFuncs()` also installs `shell.CommandsBlocker(bannedCommands)`, so even a model that tries is stopped.

Both read from the same hardcoded `var bannedCommands` in `internal/agent/tools/bash.go`. Nothing in `crush.json` or a `crushrc` reaches either one — we checked the config surface before filing.

## On the wrapper workaround

> I did an SSH wrapper in 20 seconds and it works just fine.

That works, and that is the problem. If a 20-second rename restores the capability, the ban is not a security boundary — it is friction. What it actually costs:

- The stated policy and the effective policy diverge. An operator reading `bannedCommands` believes `ssh` is unreachable; it is not.
- The model has to be told the wrapper exists, so the workaround leaks into every prompt.
- Nothing is audited. A first-class config option would at least be greppable in the config, and reviewable.

A knob that says "yes, I mean it" is both safer and more honest than a ban that everyone routes around.

## What would help

`permissions allow`/`deny` already exists in the config and is honoured — the banned list sits outside it as a separate, non-overridable layer. Folding the two together, or adding an explicit override, would make the model consistent:

```jsonc
{
  "permissions": {
    // opt in explicitly; empty/absent keeps today's behaviour
    "allow_banned_commands": ["ssh", "scp", "systemctl"]
  }
}
```

Defaulting to the current list is right. The ask is only that an operator who has already said "never ask me" at every other layer can say it here too.

Happy to test a branch against the fleet deployment if that is useful.

Reconciled this branch with the A2UI fixes that landed downstream after the payload commit was cut. Seven commits on top of `7f9e85e3b`, each a self-contained fix with the coverage that catches it.

### Correctness fixes

**`fix(mcp): honor the ["assistant"]-only A2UI audience`** — the audience annotation collapsed to a single "may the model see this" bit, so the render decision fell out of `divert` alone. Two shapes came out wrong: an `["assistant"]` surface was rendered for the user anyway, and a `["user"]` surface was withheld from the model even when nothing was rendering it — in a headless `crush run`, or with `disable_a2ui`, a tool whose only content was a `["user"]` surface handed back an empty result and the agent answered with nothing. Now resolved into both bits, and the payload folds back to the model whenever no renderer exists.

**`fix(a2ui): never route an assistant surface to an MCP server`** — surface IDs are only unique within whatever authored them, and `"default"` is the common choice on both sides. On a collision, both provenance lookups resolved in the server's favour: the user's form values were shipped to that server's `a2ui_action` tool, the surface was never retired, and no agent turn started. The button just looked dead.

**`fix(a2ui): publish a2ui_* capability so remote clients can round-trip`** — `mcp.HasTool` reads the process-global tool registry, which only exists where the MCP sessions live. In client/server mode the TUI is not that process, so every `HasTool` gate was permanently false and the entire A2UI action round-trip silently never fired, leaving the `/mcp/call-tool` route this PR adds unreachable. The `a2ui_*` names now ride on the published MCP state (`ClientInfo.A2UITools` → `MCPClientInfo.a2ui_tools`); only that subset travels, since a full catalog per server on every state change would be a lot of wire for nothing. `HasTool` and `SetToolsForTest` had no other callers and are gone.

**`fix(a2ui): rebuild tool surfaces on restyle, and never cache a live frame`** — two ways a tool-held surface got stuck. `buildA2UISurfaces` bakes the active theme's `render.Styles` into each model, and `clearCache` is only reached from the theme-change path, so a surviving surface kept drawing the old palette beside newly-themed chat. Separately, `Render` decided cache-eligibility *before* `RawRender` had built the surfaces, so the "don't cache a live surface" guard was still false on the first frame — and since `getCachedPrefixedRender` keys on `(width, prefix)` alone, once the server deleted the surface that dead frame was replayed for the rest of the item's life.

**`fix(mcp): re-register resource templates on renewal, report listing errors`** — `getOrRenewClient` re-listed plain resources but not resource templates, and A2UI surfaces are served through templates, so after any reconnect every surface URI vanished from `@` completions until restart. The listing error is now returned rather than swallowed: on the renewal path it is fatal exactly as it already is for tools and prompts, because publishing `StateConnected` over it shows a healthy server whose resources have all disappeared. The startup path still ignores it explicitly — a server that hangs on `resources/list` must not stall `WaitForInit`.

### Docs

**`docs(a2ui): teach the resource-read path in the skill and system prompt`** — both described only the inline path, so a model facing a server that already serves the view reconstructed it by hand. Both now lead with the two delivery paths and prefer reading an `/a2ui` resource for server-owned data. The prompt also picks up the rules that were skill-only (flat adjacency list, `Button` label as a child `Text`, no code in surfaces, host-managed `?w=`) and drops the claim that input components render read-only — a button press harvests their values and submits them, so that line talked the model out of a working feature.

That section is gated by `{{if .A2UI}}` and A2UI is off in `TestCoderAgent`'s config, so no cassette pins the text. Hence the added coverage asserting it names only registered tools and agrees with the skill on input editability.

Happy to regenerate if you would rather take the drift in one go.

Second reconcile pass against the downstream fork, now that the A2UI capability advertisement has been reviewed and merged there. Five more commits.

The headline: **crush renders A2UI but never declares that it can.** Per the [A2UI-over-MCP capability negotiation](https://a2ui.org/guides/a2ui_over_mcp/), a server checks the client's `capabilities.a2ui` before sending surfaces, so a spec-compliant server is entitled to withhold them from a client that stays silent. The inverse matters too: a deployment with `options.disable_a2ui` set must actively say it *cannot* render, and today it makes no statement either way.

### The capability layer

- **`feat(mcp): advertise capabilities.a2ui at MCP initialize`** — an `a2uiInitTransport` connection wrapper merges the capability into the serialized initialize params, namespaced by `a2ui.Version` with the compiled-in basic catalog ID, so the advertised capability, the coder prompt, and the renderer share one source of truth. Stateless servers that can't carry initialize-time state get it per-call in `_meta` instead. Both gated on `disable_a2ui`.
- **`fix(mcp): make the a2ui capability reach servers and match what crush renders`** — the review round on the above. The capability was being **dropped on receipt** by go-sdk servers: the wire injection was correct, but a go-sdk peer unmarshals capabilities into a typed struct with no `a2ui` field and no catch-all, so the top-level key vanished. It now sends both the spec's top-level key and the SDK's Extensions map, because neither alone reaches everyone. Also stops claiming the capability on turns that will not render.
- **`fix(mcp): read the A2UI opt-out without assuming Options is populated`** — `Config.Options` is a pointer, and reading `cfg.Config().Options.DisableA2UI` inside `createSession` panics on any path where a config exists but `Options` was never populated. All opt-out reads now go through one nil-tolerant helper.

**Note on technique:** the go-sdk's typed `ClientCapabilities` has no slot for the spec's *top-level* `a2ui` key, so the transport wrapper is how the capability gets on the wire at all — the same seam `channelTransport` already uses. If you'd rather not carry that, this is isolated in its own commit and droppable without disturbing anything else in the PR.

### Two bugs that are yours, not A2UI's

Both surfaced while porting, both reproduce on `main` today, and both are independent of this feature — happy to split them into their own PR if you'd prefer them separately.

- **`fix(mcp): don't duplicate argv0 when re-running a failed stdio server`** — `stdioCheck` builds its diagnostic re-run as `exec.CommandContext(ctx, old.Path, old.Args...)`, but `Cmd.Args` already carries argv0 and `CommandContext` prepends `Path` as argv0 itself. So a failed `npx -y pkg` is re-run as `npx npx -y pkg`, and the joined error reports whatever that malformed command produced (`cannot execute binary file`) instead of the child's real startup output — exactly the message `stdioCheck` exists to surface.

- **`fix(mcp): drop resource templates when a server dies`** — `updateState`'s `StateError` arm and `clearMCPData` clear tools, prompts, and resources, but not the resource-template registry. A2UI surfaces are served through templates, so an errored or torn-down server keeps offering its surface URIs in the `@` completions popup — the same "advertising capabilities the agent can no longer fulfil" divergence the surrounding code already prevents for tools.

- `go test -race -failfast ./...` green; `golangci-lint run` 0 issues.
- `schema.json` regenerated from this branch (the downstream copy carried config fields that don't exist here).
- The transport unwrap is what makes `stdioCheck` reachable through a wrapped transport at all, so `maybeStdioErr` now unwraps generically over a `transportWrapper` interface both decorators implement — a future wrapper can't silently re-break stdio diagnostics.

Final review pass on `059ba81`, run as a self-review before asking anyone to merge this. I checked out the branch and exercised `isSafeReadOnly` directly rather than reasoning from the diff, so everything below is an observed return value.

**The thesis holds.** Every bypass this PR claims to close does close: `echo hi > /tmp/x`, `env -S ls`, `env --split-string=ls`, `git config --get-urlmatch a b` and `git diff --ext-diff` all return `false`, `PATH=/tmp/evil ls` returns `false`, and `ls; pwd` correctly returns `true`. Fail-closed behaviour on subshells, loops and parse errors is as described. CI is green across all 15 checks.

But there are four places where the new matcher still auto-approves something it shouldn't, and one of them undercuts the PR's own stated invariant. **I don't think this should merge as-is.**

To be clear up front: *none of these four are regressions.* All four also auto-approve on current `main` under the prefix matcher, so this branch is still strictly an improvement. The reason I'm flagging them anyway is that a change whose argument is "auto-approve only what is provably inert" should not leave a known-not-inert case on the list — that's a weaker promise than the code now appears to make.

### 1. `env NAME=VALUE cmd` reopens the assignment vector — blocking

`safeStmt` rejects `call.Assigns` with the comment that assignments "can steer the command through its environment (PATH, LD_PRELOAD, GIT_*)". `peelWrapper` then accepts the same assignments when they're spelled through `env`, because of `allowAssigns: true`:

```
isSafeReadOnly("env PATH=/tmp/evil ls")                      => true
isSafeReadOnly("env LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/evil.so ls")             => true
isSafeReadOnly("env GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF=/tmp/evil git diff")   => true
isSafeReadOnly("env GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/tmp/evil git status") => true
isSafeReadOnly("nice -n 5 env PATH=/tmp/evil ls")            => true

isSafeReadOnly("PATH=/tmp/evil ls")                          => false   # control
```

`GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF` runs an arbitrary program on the first changed file — which is precisely what `--ext-diff` is on `gitCodeExecFlags` to prevent, arriving by another door. `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` can point `core.fsmonitor` at a program that `git status` then runs.

What makes this worth blocking on rather than filing as a follow-up is that the tests pin both halves of the contradiction: `safe_test.go:128` asserts `PATH=/evil ls` is unsafe, and `safe_test.go:172` asserts `env FOO=bar ls` peels to a bare `ls`. So the invariant is documented as held in one file and asserted away in another.

Simplest fix is to drop `allowAssigns` entirely — `env FOO=bar cmd` then costs a prompt, consistent with the bare prefix form. Happy to push that plus a test.

### 2. `--textconv` isn't on `gitCodeExecFlags`

```
isSafeReadOnly("git diff --textconv")      => true
isSafeReadOnly("git show --textconv HEAD") => true
```

A textconv driver is a repo-configured program that git executes, same as an external diff driver. In a repository the user cloned but doesn't control, this is `--ext-diff` by another name. It belongs on the list.

### 3. `denyFlags` misses attached and clustered short options

`flagName` splits on `=` only, so a short flag carrying its value inline never matches its deny entry:

```
isSafeReadOnly("date -s2020-01-01")    => true   # "-s" is on date's deny list
isSafeReadOnly("date -us 2020-01-01")  => true   # clustered
isSafeReadOnly("hostname -F/tmp/evil") => true   # attached value, so no operand
```

`hostname -F/tmp/evil` is the interesting shape: because the value is attached there's no separate operand token, so `allowOperands: false` never fires. Both need privileges to take effect, but the deny doesn't hold as written. For single-dash tokens, comparing the leading two characters against the deny/allow sets as well as the whole token would cover it.

### 4. `git remote show` reaches the network

```
isSafeReadOnly("git remote show origin") => true
```

That makes the two forms agree, which is the actual point: `FOO=bar ls` and `env FOO=bar ls` now both prompt, rather than one being rejected by `safeStmt` and the other waved through by `peelWrapper`.

`env` keeps its other behaviour — `env ls`, `env -i ls`, `env -u PATH ls` still auto-approve.

### 2. `--textconv`

Added to `gitCodeExecFlags`, with a comment tying it to `--ext-diff`: both run a program the repository's own config names, so a repo the user cloned but doesn't control picks what executes.

### 3. Attached and clustered short flags

`denyFlags` matching moved into a `flagDenied` helper. A long flag still matches by name (`--output=x` → `--output`); a single-dash token now also gets read character by character, since getopt accepts both `-s2020-01-01` and `-us` for a flag the list spells `-s`.

`hostname` needed a different fix rather than the same one — it has no deny list, and the write flag takes its value attached (`hostname -F/etc/x`), so there's no operand for `allowOperands: false` to catch. It moves to `restrictFlags` with an enumerated read-only set (`-f`, `-s`, `-d`, `-i`, `-I`, `-A`, `-a`, `-y` and long forms). Bare `hostname` and `hostname -f` still auto-approve; anything unrecognized, including a cluster of otherwise-allowed shorts, fails closed.

Deliberately left `restrictFlags` matching exact. Making the allow path cluster-aware would *loosen* it — `-l` being allowed would start admitting `-ln9` — so the permissive reading belongs only on the deny path.

Now `restrictFlags` + `requireFlag` on `-n`. `git remote show -n origin` auto-approves; `git remote show origin` prompts, since without `-n` it does a live `ls-remote` against the configured URL — the behaviour cited for keeping `git ls-remote` off the list.

**Verdict: strong direction, one blocking bug.** Parsing instead of prefix-matching is the right call, the fail-closed structure is clean, and every bypass listed in the description does now prompt — I checked each one. One evasion survives, and one residual risk is worth documenting because the description implies it is covered.

## Blocking: backslash escapes defeat every deny-flag check

`literalWord` copies `syntax.Lit.Value` verbatim, but `Lit.Value` keeps unquoted backslash
escapes, so the string it computes is *not* the argv the shell will pass. Anything protected
by `denyFlags` can be spelled with one backslash and auto-approves:

```
"git diff --ext\-diff"        => true    # runs repo-configured external diff driver
"git diff --outpu\t=/tmp/x"   => true    # arbitrary file write
"git log --text\conv"         => true
"date --se\t 2020-01-01"      => true
```

Confirmed the interpreter Crush actually uses expands these: `echo --outpu\t=x` →
`--output=x`. `argv[0]` is unaffected (`\ls` fails closed), so the impact is limited to
exactly the flags this PR added to stop code execution and file writes.

Minimal fix, in `internal/agent/tools/safe.go` (`literalWord`, the `*syntax.Lit` case):

```go
case *syntax.Lit:
	if strings.Contains(p.Value, `\`) {
		return "", false
	}
	sb.WriteString(p.Value)
```

Applied locally: all four probes flip to `false` and the existing suite still passes.
(Double-quoted `Lit` parts have the same verbatim-backslash property, so covering both with
one check is correct and only ever fails closed.) Worth a regression case per deny-flag
entry. See "Interaction with #2831" below for a better long-term fix.

## Residual risk: `git diff` executes repo config regardless of flags

Denying `--ext-diff`/`--textconv` reads as if external drivers are handled, but plain
`git diff` honors `diff.external` from the repository's own `.git/config`. Verified in a
throwaway repo — bare `git diff`, no flags, ran the configured script:

```
git config diff.external ./evil.sh && git diff   # evil.sh runs
```

Same for `.gitattributes` textconv drivers. Not a regression (`git diff` was already
auto-approved on `main`), and not fixable via flag policy since the matcher only
approves/denies rather than rewriting the command. But the entry's comment should say so,
otherwise the next reader assumes the flag list closes this.

## Non-blocking

- **Over-restriction on common reads.** `git tag -l 'v*'`, `git branch --list 'feature/*'`,
  `git config --get-regexp x` now prompt. The pattern operand to `--list`/`-l` is read-only;
  consider a third entry mirroring the `--contains` pattern with
  `allowFlags: {-l, --list}`, `requireFlag: true`, `allowOperands: true`.
- **Char-scanning short flags fails closed on attached values**: `date -Iseconds` prompts
  because the value contains `s`. The tradeoff is documented in `flagDenied`, just noting
  it's user-visible.
- **`peelWrapper` accepts flags after the wrapper's operands**: `timeout 5 --foo ls` peels
  to `ls` and approves, though the shell would run `--foo`. Harmless (the executed command
  doesn't exist), but the peel diverges from real argv there.
- **Case-insensitivity dropped**: `LS`, `Git status` previously auto-approved, now prompt.
  Fine, worth a line in the behavior-changes list since it's not mentioned.
- **Secret exposure is outside the stated bar.** `printenv`, `env`, `git config --list`,
  `git remote get-url` auto-approve and can dump provider API keys or credential-bearing
  remote URLs into model context. Pre-existing, not this PR's job, but the membership rule
  ("cannot write, mutate, execute, or reach the network") should probably grow a
  read-secrets clause.
- **`TimeClause` recursion in `safeStmt` is unbounded** while wrapper peeling is capped at
  4. Practically unreachable (the parser recurses first), just inconsistent.
- **Convention**: `safe_test.go` is the only file in `internal/agent/tools` using
  `testify/assert`; the rest and AGENTS.md use `require`.

## What's good

- Wrapper peeling with the inner command re-checked on its own merits is the right model,
  and leaving `env FOO=bar` assignments in the inner argv so they fail closed is a nice
  touch.
- Rejecting substitutions rather than evaluating them, and the comment on `echo` explaining
  it's only safe while redirections are rejected, are exactly the notes a future editor
  needs.
- Removing `kill`/`killall`/`set`/`unset`/`git ls-remote`/`ping` is well argued; the README
  paragraph accurately describes the new behavior.
- Tests are thorough and readable; `go test ./internal/agent/tools/` and `go vet` are clean
  on this branch.

## Interaction with #2831 (sysadmin mode)

#2831 touches the same three files and reworks the surrounding policy, so the two need to be
sequenced deliberately. Summary of how they meet:

**They will conflict textually.** #2831 keeps `safeCommands []string` and rewrites
`containsCommandChaining` as a thin shim over a new AST-based
`shell.ContainsCommandChaining`; its `safe_test.go` tests that helper directly. #3426 deletes
both. Landing #3426 first is the cheaper order — #2831 is 69 files and already
`mergeable_state: dirty` — after which #2831 should drop its shim and the
`shell.ContainsCommandChaining` helper entirely (its only consumer is `safe.go`), keep
`shell.IsCommandBlocked` (still needed for the new `Dangerous` flag), and call
`isSafeReadOnly` at the same spot.

**#3426 fixes a hole that #2831 leaves open and codifies.**
`shell.ContainsCommandChaining` deliberately treats redirection as non-chaining
("`ls > out` changes where output goes, not which commands run"), which is only true if the
command is *also* verified to be redirect-free. It isn't: with #2831 alone,
`echo pwned > ~/.bashrc` still matches the `echo` prefix, still auto-approves, and `echo`
isn't on the block list, so nothing stops it. #3426 is what closes that.

**#2831 makes the safe list the last unguarded path.** #2831 stops applying the exec-time
block list to anything that went through a prompt (approval is the gate) and keeps it *only*
on the safe-read-only branch, explicitly as "a backstop against a dangerous command smuggled
past the safe-prefix match." That raises the stakes on #3426's correctness in a useful way,
but note the backstop does not cover the escape bug above: it matches `argv[0]` of the
command the model wrote, and `git diff --ext\-diff` has `argv[0] == "git"`. The program that
actually executes is chosen by the repository's config, so the bypass stays silent even with
#2831's backstop in place. Fix the escape handling regardless of merge order.

**Concrete interaction bug to fix in whichever lands second.** #2831 adds user-facing
`permissions.blocked_commands` / `allowed_commands`, but `isSafeReadOnly` short-circuits
before the block list is consulted. A user who adds `git` to `blocked_commands` gets
`git status` auto-approved with no prompt, and then a hard "not allowed" error from the
exec-time backstop — the opposite of what they asked for, and a worse experience than a
prompt. The safe path should let the block list veto auto-approval and fall through to the
prompt:

```go
safeReadOnly := isSafeReadOnly(params.Command) &&
	!shell.IsCommandBlocked(params.Command, blockFuncs(blocked))
```

That also buys defense-in-depth against the escape bug, because `IsCommandBlocked` resolves
words through `expand.Fields` and therefore sees the real argv.

**Better long-term fix for the escape bug, borrowed from #2831.** #2831's expansion setup —
empty env, nil `CmdSubst`, erroring `ProcSubst` — is exactly the right primitive for turning
a word into its true text without executing anything. #3426 should keep its "every part must
be a literal or a plain quote" gate (needed, since resolving `$VAR` to empty would be wrong
in the *approve* direction) and then compute the text with `expand`, instead of
concatenating `Lit.Value` by hand. That removes a whole class of quoting mismatches rather
than patching backslashes specifically. Post-merge there should be one shell-analysis
helper, in `internal/shell`, not two independent parsers in two packages disagreeing about
what a command says.

**Good news on the usability regressions.** The prompts #3426 adds (`ls $HOME`,
`git tag -l 'v*'`, `git branch -D`) only bite in normal mode. Under #2831, `-y` auto-approves
everything not on the dangerous list, so yolo users never see them, and sysadmin mode skips
prompts entirely. The two PRs complement each other here: #3426 tightens the never-asks path,
#2831 gives users a supported way to opt out of asking.

This is not a leak — it's the "small model" used for background tasks. Crush uses two models: a `large` model (your chat/agent model) and a `small` model used for auxiliary tasks like session title generation and summarization. When you don't configure a small model, Crush picks one automatically, and that default is a Claude Haiku via bedrock model.

Thanks for the branch work, @4RH1T3CT0R7 — that does prove the single-knob path is viable, and your point about not having to figure out which knob applies at a given window size is fair.

That said, I'd still prefer to land the smaller diff first: two `omitempty` config fields (`auto_summarize_ratio`, `auto_summarize_buffer`) that just expose the two existing constants in `internal/agent/agent.go:57-59`. Concretely:

```json
{ "options": { "auto_summarize_ratio": 0.3, "auto_summarize_buffer": 20000 } }
```

Unset keeps today's behavior (`20%` reserve on ≤200K windows, `20K` reserve on >200K). Set fields only override their regime.

Why I'd keep both knobs rather than collapse them:

1. The two regimes aren't really the same rule. On a 1M model, `ratio=0.2` reserves 200K of headroom — that's a much bigger share of the working window than `20K of 200K` (10%) on a 200K model. A single ratio hides that the absolute cost scales with window size; the maintainers' choice to gate at `200_000` and switch units is doing real work.
2. The diff is smaller and easier to review: one `switch` over `agent.go:1046`, two new `omitempty` config fields, no constant reshuffle. Single-knob rewrites the heuristic on top of exposing it.
3. Doesn't preclude the single-knob follow-up. If the two-knob version lands, anyone can later propose collapsing it. Harder to land and revert a refactor of the threshold function in the same PR.

Happy to coordinate — if you'd rather lead with your single-knob branch I can review and add tests; if maintainers prefer the two-knob approach I'll open that one. Either way we should keep the scope narrow in this issue so #1601 / #2331 aren't blocked on us.

**Blocking — backslash escapes defeat deny-flag checks.** Confirmed: `syntax.Lit.Value` keeps unquoted escapes verbatim, so `git diff --ext\-diff` read as inert text here but ran as `--ext-diff` after the shell stripped the backslash. `literalWord` now fails closed on any `*syntax.Lit` containing a backslash, in both the bare and double-quoted cases, rather than re-implementing the shell's escape rules. Ran into the stuck-`working` symptom independently and instrumented it from the herdr side; sharing data that narrows the cause (originally filed as #3672, closing in favor of this issue / #3541).

**Setup:** herdr 0.7.5, crush TUI panes (`HERDR_ENV=1`), sampled `herdr agent get <pane>` every ~2s externally.

**Observations:**

1. **Aged sessions stop reporting, fresh ones are perfect.** A crush TUI running ~36 min finished a turn at 19:45:40 and herdr stayed `working` indefinitely (never `idle`, no further state changes). A second pane (~20 min) sat idle at the prompt for 6+ min showing `working`, and its *next* full turn produced zero state-change events — reports stopped entirely, not just the idle one. Meanwhile a freshly started TUI showed flawless `idle → working → idle` across multiple turns.

2. **herdr's pipeline is not the problem.** Manually reporting `idle` for a stuck pane via herdr's CLI flips it to done instantly, so herdr applies `pane.report_agent` idle states fine. Whatever fails is on the crush side of the socket.

3. **Suspects in `internal/herdr`:**
   - `unixSender` drops on full buffer and logs failures at `slog.Debug` only — if the writer wedges once, every later report is lost and the pane freezes on `working`. Pane B's "no events at all for a whole turn" pattern fits this better than a one-off ordering race.
   - The `AssistantMessage` → `working` / `RunComplete` → `idle` pairing can interleave badly with background small-model runs (title generation), which emit on the same brokers.

4. **Non-interactive oddity:** `crush run` inside a herdr pane sent `pane.release_agent` ~1 s after startup while still running, leaving the pane agent-less for the whole run.

Happy to retest on a clean checkout or with the #3541 branch once reviewable.

The stable-prefix cache on streaming markdown can only advance to a **blank line** (`blankLineBefore` requires `\n\n`). A reasoning trace holding no blank line never yields a boundary, so every flush falls through to `full()`: a complete glamour parse of the whole accumulated document, thirty times a second. Quadratic in trace length with no ceiling.

Measured locally, a trace grown to 141 KB over 2000 flushes:

| trace shape | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| blank line every 10 lines | 0.80 GB | 0.80 GB (unchanged) |
| no blank lines | **19.67 GB** | **1.67 GB** |

That 19.67 GB is identical to what v0.79.0 did. 3295a085c (v0.81.0) fixed the case it was tested against and left the pathological one exactly as it was.

It fits every number in the report: anonymous heap only, file-rss under 2 MB, single process, roughly a minute to OOM, and "the TUI is also very laggy" is the same CPU burn seen from the other side. Both providers in that config, DeepSeek and Xiaomi MiMo, are long-reasoning models. Same class as #2918. The part that stings is `maxCollapsedThinkingHeight = 10`: a collapsed thinking box was re-rendering 141 KB of markdown per tick to show ten lines.

**The fix.** Past 8 KB of unstable tail, cut at a plain newline and validate it with `isSafeBoundaryIncremental`, the same predicate the blank-line search already uses. Every hazard check survives: `lineOpensConstruct` rejects any line containing a pipe so tables never split, fence parity keeps cuts out of code blocks, and lists, block quotes, indented code and setext all still bail. The only conservatism given up is paragraph wrapping across the cut, and only where prose has outgrown it. Below the threshold nothing changes at all.

Tests cover relaxed advance on 400 lines of blank-line-free prose, plus a hazard table asserting `stablePrefix` stays empty for a 1200-row table and for an open code fence.

**Known gaps, not addressed here:**

- Content with no newline at all has nothing to cut on and stays on the full-render path. Cutting mid-line would break wrapping visibly.
- `glueRenders` still rebuilds the whole rendered document as a string every tick, so there is an inherent O(n) memcpy per flush. About 30 MB/s on a 500 KB trace at 30fps. That is why the 1.67 GB is not flat.
- Separately: `pubsub.bufferSize` is 4096 per subscriber, and each queued `UpdatedEvent` pins a distinct generation of the growing message. A stalled consumer holds 4096 snapshots of the same accumulated string, so it is bounded in count but not in bytes. The package doc says only the latest state matters, so a deep queue of superseded frames buys nothing, but shrinking it trades worst-case memory against `PublishMustDeliver` timing out sooner under a sustained stall. Worth its own PR.

> If pre-commit hook fails, retry ONCE. If fails again, hook preventing commit. If succeeds but files modified, MUST amend.

This PR's wording ("If the first attempt succeeds, generating a commit, but files modified, the next attempt MUST amend") is the right direction but still does not name the guard: only amend a commit Crush just created.

> 6. If the pre-commit hook fails, retry ONCE with a new `git commit` (not `--amend`). If the retry fails, stop — the hook is preventing the commit. If a commit this attempt created succeeded but the hook modified files, `git commit --amend` **that new commit only**. Never `--amend` a commit that already existed before this attempt (record `git rev-parse HEAD` before the first commit; refuse to amend if HEAD is still that SHA).

Reporter's perspective on the design question, since the fail-loud shape came out of #3671:

A config opt-out was considered and deliberately not requested. The failure this fixes is silent contamination in CI/benchmarks — and config files are exactly the thing that gets copied between environments. An opt-out living in the config means the unsafe behavior travels with the config; six months later nobody remembers it's set, and we're back to the original incident (a multi-day benchmark series silently running the wrong model).

A one-release deprecation warning has the problem stated in #3671: the affected class of user (headless CI) doesn't read stderr until the runs are already spent — the warning release delays the protection without reaching anyone who needs it.

`-m` as the only escape is the intended shape: it's per-invocation and visible at the call site, so an override is always explicit in the one place someone will look when results are surprising.

Your implementation points (shared helper, nil-key guard, GetConfig error swallow) all look right to me — those are for @kvnloo.

Update: this fix has now been **validated in production**, and I have a data point that may be useful when weighing it.

We run a homegrown streamable-HTTP MCP server that pushes work notifications to channel-enabled clients. Before the fix, every push was rejected server-side:

```
doorbell delivered: 0
doorbell dropped:   4
err="rejected by transport: undelivered message: stream not connected or already closed"
```

After deploying this change to four consumers across two hosts:

```
doorbell delivered: 6
doorbell dropped:   0
```

and the agents began completing pushed work end to end for the first time.

Two things I learned that are worth recording here, because both cost real time:

**The failure is completely silent from the client.** The session initializes, `tools/call` works, and pings are answered over ordinary POSTs, so every liveness signal reads healthy while no server-initiated notification can ever arrive. There is no error anywhere — the `ok` from the type assertion is discarded. Diagnosing it required server-side logging of the *delivery outcome*; nothing on the client side hints at it.

**A test that constructs `channelTransport` directly will not catch it.** Mine did, and passed throughout, because the property depends on what `createSession` hands the SDK rather than on `channelTransport` in isolation. If any other transport wrapper is ever added around this one, it will silently reintroduce the bug — in our fork we hit exactly that: a second wrapper applied one line later put the wrapper straight back and undid the fix. Worth considering a test that asserts the stream opens through the full wrapper stack, not just this transport, if you take the change.
